title: The American Revolution
desc: The American Revolution was the war in which the 13 colonies broke away from Britain and became the United States. Fighting began in 1775 and ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, which recognized American independence.
prompts: why did the colonies fight britain
what war created the united states
when did the american revolution end

title: The Declaration of Independence
desc: The Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776, announced that the 13 colonies were separating from Britain. It says that people have rights such as life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and it lists complaints against the British king. Thomas Jefferson was its main author.
prompts: what is the declaration of independence
when was the declaration of independence signed
who wrote the declaration of independence
life liberty and the pursuit of happiness
why was the declaration of independence written

title: The U.S. Constitution
desc: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the United States. Written in 1787, it sets up the national government, divides power among branches and states, and describes the rights of the people, including later amendments.
prompts: supreme law of the united states

title: The three branches of government
desc: The U.S. federal government has three branches. Congress, the legislative branch, makes laws. The president and the executive branch carry out laws. The courts, the judicial branch, interpret laws and the Constitution.
prompts: what are the three branches of government
who makes the laws in the united states
what does the president do in government
what does the judicial branch do

title: How a bill becomes a law
desc: A bill is introduced in the House or Senate, studied in committee, and must pass both chambers in the same form. The president can sign it into law or veto it. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
prompts: how does a bill become a law
how can congress override a veto
what happens after a bill passes both houses
steps for a bill to become law
who signs a bill into law
committee and then the full house

title: The Bill of Rights
desc: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791. It protects freedoms such as speech, religion, the press, assembly and petition, and it also covers rights such as a jury trial and protection from unreasonable searches.
prompts: what is the bill of rights
what are the first ten amendments
when was the bill of rights ratified
what rights are in the bill of rights
does the bill of rights include a jury trial

title: Voting in the United States
desc: In the United States, citizens who are 18 or older can vote once they meet their state's registration rules. People vote in local, state and federal elections. Rules about registration, ID and early or mail voting vary by state, so check your state or local election office.
prompts: how does voting work in the united states
who can vote in the us
how old do you have to be to vote
how do i register to vote
do voting rules differ by state

title: The Electoral College
desc: The Electoral College is the system used to elect the U.S. president. There are 538 electors, and a candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to win. Each state's electors usually equal its members of Congress. In most states, the candidate who wins the statewide popular vote gets all of that state's electors.
prompts: how many electoral votes do you need to win
why isn't the president chosen only by popular vote

title: The Civil War
desc: The American Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865 between the Union and the Confederate states that had seceded. Slavery and its expansion were at the center of the conflict. The Union won, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery in the United States.
prompts: when was the american civil war
who fought in the civil war
why was the civil war fought
when did the civil war end

title: The civil rights movement
desc: The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s was a struggle to end legal racial segregation and protect equal rights for Black Americans. It included court cases, boycotts, sit-ins, marches and new laws such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
prompts: what was the civil rights movement
what did the civil rights act do
what was the voting rights act
why were there sit-ins and marches
what did the civil rights movement achieve

title: World War I
desc: World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918 and was fought mainly in Europe between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The United States entered in 1917 on the Allied side. An armistice on November 11, 1918, ended the fighting.
prompts: who fought in world war one
when did the us enter world war 1

title: World War II
desc: World War II lasted from 1939 to 1945 and was fought between the Allies and the Axis powers, including Nazi Germany, Italy and Japan. The United States entered after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. The war in Europe ended in May 1945, and Japan surrendered in September 1945.
prompts: why did the us enter world war 2
who were the allied and axis powers

title: The Industrial Revolution
desc: The Industrial Revolution was a period when many goods began to be made by machines in factories instead of by hand. It began in Britain in the 1700s and spread to other countries. Steam power, new machines and later electricity changed work, cities and transportation.
prompts: when did the industrial revolution start
why is the industrial revolution important
goods made by machines instead of by hand

title: Ancient Egypt
desc: Ancient Egypt was a civilization along the Nile River in northeast Africa. It is known for pharaohs, pyramids, hieroglyphic writing and a religion that included many gods and a strong focus on the afterlife. The Nile's yearly flooding helped farming in a desert region.
prompts: what is ancient egypt known for
why was the nile important to egypt

title: Ancient Rome
desc: Ancient Rome began as a city in Italy, became a republic, and later an empire that controlled much of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Roman law, roads, Latin and republican ideas influenced later governments. The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.
prompts: when did the western roman empire fall
rome as a republic then an empire
what language did the romans speak

title: Ancient Greece
desc: Ancient Greece was made up of city-states such as Athens and Sparta, rather than one single country. Athens is known for an early form of democracy, and Greek thinkers, writers and athletes influenced later science, government, theater and the Olympic Games.
prompts: where did the olympic games begin

title: The Silk Road
desc: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes that linked East Asia with Central Asia, the Middle East and the Mediterranean for many centuries. Merchants traded goods such as silk, spices and metals, and the routes also spread ideas, technologies and religions.
prompts: what was traded on the silk road
did the silk road spread ideas
trade routes from china to the mediterranean
why is it called the silk road
how did the silk road work

title: The Supreme Court
desc: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It has nine justices who are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, and they can serve for life. The Court interprets the Constitution and can strike down laws that conflict with it.
prompts: how many justices are on the supreme court
what does the supreme court do
can the supreme court strike down a law
highest court in the united states

title: Constitutional amendments
desc: A constitutional amendment is a formal change to the U.S. Constitution. There are 27 amendments so far. The usual process is a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress, then approval by three-fourths of the states.
prompts: two thirds of congress and three fourths of the states
how do you change the constitution

title: Checks and balances
desc: Checks and balances are ways each branch of the U.S. government can limit the others so that one branch does not become too powerful. Examples include the president's veto, Congress overriding a veto, the Senate confirming appointments, and the courts reviewing laws.
prompts: how do the branches limit each other
veto and override as a check
why do we have checks and balances

title: The Great Depression
desc: The Great Depression was a severe worldwide economic downturn that began in the United States after the stock market crash of 1929. Many people lost jobs, homes and savings. In the U.S., President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal created programs to provide relief and reform the financial system.
prompts: when did the great depression start

title: The moon landing
desc: On July 20, 1969, NASA's Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the Moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the lunar surface while Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module. Armstrong's first words included, "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."
prompts: who was the first person on the moon
when did people first walk on the moon
one small step for a man

title: Metaphor and simile
desc: A simile compares two things using like or as, such as "the cloud was like a cotton ball." A metaphor says one thing is another to make a comparison, such as "the cloud was a cotton ball." Both are figures of speech, but only a simile uses like or as.
prompts: what's the difference between a metaphor and a simile
the cloud was a cotton ball

title: Plot
desc: Plot is the sequence of events in a story. Many stories move from exposition, where the setup is introduced, through rising action and a climax, then falling action and a resolution. The conflict, the main problem the characters face, drives the plot forward.
prompts: what is plot in a story
what are the parts of a plot
what is the climax of a story
what is conflict in a story

title: Irony
desc: Irony is when the result or meaning is the opposite of what was expected or said. Verbal irony is saying one thing and meaning another. Situational irony is when events turn out the opposite of what you would expect. Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not.
prompts: when the audience knows something the character doesn't

title: MLA citations
desc: MLA style is often used in English and the humanities. A typical in-text citation is the author's last name and a page number in parentheses, such as (Lopez 12). At the end, a Works Cited list gives full details so a reader can find each source.
prompts: how do i cite a source in mla
what is a works cited page

title: APA citations
desc: APA style is often used in the social sciences. A typical in-text citation is the author's last name and the year, such as (Lopez, 2023). At the end, a References list gives full details for each source. Page numbers are added when you quote a specific passage.
prompts: how do i cite a source in apa
what is a references list in apa

title: Test-taking strategies
desc: Read the directions and skim the test so you can budget your time. Answer the questions you know first, then return to harder ones. For multiple choice, try to think of the answer before looking at the options, and cross out choices you know are wrong. Check your work if time remains.
prompts: how should i take a test
how do i manage time on a test
should i skip hard questions and come back
how can i do better on exams
what to do if i get stuck on a question
how to review answers before turning in

title: Making a study schedule
desc: List upcoming due dates and exams, then break each subject into short study sessions across several days instead of one long cram. Put the hardest or earliest work first, include breaks, and leave a little buffer for things that take longer than expected.
prompts: how do i make a study schedule
how should i plan for exams
making a homework and test schedule

title: Annotating a text
desc: Annotating means marking a text as you read to help you understand it. Underline key claims, circle words to look up, and write short notes or questions in the margin. Mark only the most useful parts so the page stays readable.
prompts: what does annotating a text mean
how do i annotate a reading
what should i write in the margins
how to mark up an article

title: Writing an essay outline
desc: An outline is a plan for your essay. Start with your thesis, then list each body paragraph's main point and the evidence you will use. Add a note for the introduction and conclusion. A clear outline makes the draft faster and helps you stay on topic.
prompts: how do i write an essay outline
how should i plan an essay

title: Introductions and conclusions
desc: An introduction should present the topic and end with your thesis, the main claim the essay will support. A conclusion should not just copy the introduction. It should tie the points together and leave the reader with the significance of your argument, without adding a major new claim.
prompts: how do i write an introduction
how do i write a conclusion
what is a thesis in an introduction
should a conclusion repeat the intro

title: Avoiding plagiarism
desc: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. Put borrowed wording in quotation marks, cite the source, and paraphrase in your own words instead of only swapping a few terms. When you are unsure, cite. Your school's policy explains the rules and consequences.
prompts: do i have to cite a paraphrase
is changing a few words enough
when should i use quotation marks

title: Do Not Disturb
desc: Do Not Disturb, or Focus modes on iPhone, can silence calls, alerts and notifications so you can sleep or work. You can usually allow repeated calls or notifications from chosen people. Check that it turns off when you want, or set a schedule so it does not stay on by accident.
prompts: what is focus mode on iphone
why am i not getting calls
how do i turn off do not disturb

title: AirDrop
desc: AirDrop is Apple's way to send photos, files and links between nearby Apple devices over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, without using a cable. Set AirDrop to receive from Everyone for a few minutes or only from Contacts, then turn it back if you do not want requests from strangers.
prompts: how do i send a photo with airdrop

title: iCloud
desc: iCloud is Apple's cloud service for backing up an iPhone and syncing photos, files and settings across your Apple devices. A backup can help you restore a new or reset phone. Photos and files in iCloud count toward your storage plan, so check Settings if you run out of space.
prompts: why is my icloud storage full
how do i back up my iphone to icloud
icloud versus on my iphone storage

title: Low Power Mode
desc: Low Power Mode on iPhone reduces background activity and some visual effects to make the remaining battery last longer. Your phone may fetch mail less often and dim features until you charge it or turn the mode off. It is useful when you cannot charge soon, not as an everyday setting for everyone.
prompts: how do i save battery on my iphone
does low power mode slow down my phone
when should i use low power mode
how to turn on low power mode
why does my iphone go into low power mode

title: Find My
desc: Find My can help you locate a missing iPhone, iPad, Mac or AirTag on a map, play a sound, or mark the device as lost. It works best when the device is powered on and connected, and when Find My was already turned on. A lost mode can lock the device and show a message with a contact number.
prompts: how do i find a lost iphone
how does find my iphone work
can i find my phone if it's dead
play a sound on a missing phone

title: Offloading apps
desc: Offloading an app removes the app from your phone but keeps its documents and data. You get the storage back that the app itself used, and you can reinstall it later without starting all over. Deleting an app can also remove its data, so offload if you think you will need that data again.
prompts: how do i free space without losing app data
remove an app but keep its documents

title: Screen Time
desc: Screen Time on iPhone shows how long you use apps and can set limits, downtime or a passcode so a younger user cannot just change the rules. Use it to see where time goes and to set limits you actually want, and keep the passcode different from your device passcode if you are setting limits for yourself.
prompts: what is screen time on iphone
how do i set app limits
how can i see how much i use my phone

title: Restarting a frozen phone
desc: If an iPhone is frozen, first try a regular restart: press and hold a volume button and the side button, then slide to power off, wait, and turn it back on. If the screen will not respond, use a force restart: quickly press volume up, then volume down, then hold the side button until the Apple logo appears.
prompts: how do i restart a frozen iphone
how do i force restart an iphone
volume up volume down hold side button
how to reboot a stuck phone

title: Freeing phone storage
desc: On iPhone, open Settings, then General, then iPhone Storage to see what is using space. Large videos, downloaded files and unused apps are common. Offload unused apps, delete videos you already backed up, and clear downloads in Safari or Files. Restart after large deletions if the free space has not updated yet.
prompts: how do i free up storage on my iphone
why is my iphone storage full
what is using space on my phone
how to make space on my phone
where is iphone storage in settings

title: Mobile hotspots
desc: A mobile hotspot lets other devices use your phone's cellular data as Wi-Fi. It can use up data quickly and drain the battery, and some plans charge extra or cap hotspot data. Use a password, turn the hotspot off when you are done, and avoid it if you are low on data.
prompts: how do i share my phone's internet
does a hotspot use my data
how to turn on a hotspot
why is my hotspot using so much data

title: Screen mirroring
desc: Screen mirroring shows your phone or computer display on a TV or monitor. AirPlay works with Apple devices and many compatible TVs, and some TVs or apps also support Chromecast or an HDMI cable. Both devices usually need to be on the same Wi-Fi network, except when you use a cable.
prompts: how do i put my phone on the tv

title: USB-C and Lightning
desc: Lightning is Apple's older small charging connector used on many earlier iPhones. USB-C is a wider, reversible connector now used on newer iPhones, many Android phones, laptops and chargers. A cable has to match the ports on both ends, and charging speed also depends on the charger, not only the plug shape.
prompts: what's the difference between usb-c and lightning
why doesn't this charger fit my phone
does the cable affect charging speed

title: Strong passwords
desc: A strong password is long, unique to that account, and hard to guess. A passphrase of several unrelated words is easier to remember than a short mix of characters. Use a different password for email and banking, and a password manager can store them so you do not reuse the same one everywhere.
prompts: how do i make a strong password
how can i remember different passwords
is a short password with symbols enough

title: Two-factor authentication
desc: Two-factor authentication, or 2FA, asks for a second check after your password, such as a code from a text message or an authenticator app. It makes it much harder for someone who only has your password to get in. Keep backup codes in a safe place in case you lose your phone.
prompts: how does two factor authentication work
why do i get a login code
is 2fa safer than a password alone

title: Phishing messages
desc: A phishing message tries to trick you into sharing a password, code or payment, often by posing as a bank, school, store or delivery service. Check the real address, not just the display name, and do not tap unexpected links or share a login code. If you are unsure, open the official app or website yourself.
prompts: how can i tell if an email is a scam
someone asked for my login code
do not click a suspicious link
what should i do if i get a phishing text

title: Private browsing
desc: Private or Incognito browsing does not save your history, cookies or form entries on that device after you close the window. It does not make you invisible. Your school, workplace, internet provider or the sites you visit can still see activity, and downloads you save stay on the device.
prompts: who can still see incognito browsing

title: Browser cookies
desc: Cookies are small files a site stores in your browser to remember things such as a login, language or items in a cart. Some cookies also track visits across sites for advertising. You can usually block or clear cookies in browser settings, but you may have to log in again afterward.
prompts: what do cookies do in a browser
why do sites ask me to accept cookies
why did clearing cookies log me out
